name: Places, Cities & Housing
tagline: Where we live, where we travel, what we build
blurb: Twelve cue cards in the Quarter 3 forecast, more than any other module, plus seven Part 1 frames. Almost none of this is covered by earlier material, so the lexical set below was built for this quarter specifically.

vocab.def: the uncontrolled spread of a city into the countryside around it
vocab.n: Academic and faintly disapproving. It names a process, not a place, so it belongs in Part 3 rather than in a description of where you live.
vocab.eg: Urban sprawl has swallowed three villages that were farmland when my mother was at school.

vocab.def: to appear suddenly and in large numbers
vocab.n: Carries a sense of surprise at the speed. Used of buildings, cafés and businesses, never of people.
vocab.eg: Four tower blocks have sprung up on that road in the time I've lived here.

vocab.def: something extremely ugly in an otherwise pleasant setting
vocab.n: Strongly negative and slightly indignant. The contrast with the surroundings is part of the meaning, so it needs a setting to work against.
vocab.eg: The car park is a complete eyesore, sitting between two restored colonial buildings.

vocab.vi: vô hồn, không có bản sắc
vocab.n: The precise word for modern architecture that works but moves nobody. Far stronger evidence of lexical range than boring or not interesting.
vocab.eg: It's efficient, clean and completely soulless — you could be in any city on earth.

vocab.def: to be deeply marked by a long past
vocab.vi: đậm đặc dấu ấn lịch sử
vocab.n: Fixed in the passive with in. Slightly literary, so one use per answer; two sounds like a guidebook.
vocab.eg: The old quarter is steeped in history, though most people walk through it looking at their phones.

vocab.def: to make something neglected active and attractive again
vocab.vi: thổi luồng sinh khí mới vào
vocab.n: Positive, and the natural phrase for regeneration questions. Note the verb is breathe, not breath — a spelling error that becomes a pronunciation error.
vocab.eg: The night market has breathed new life into a street that was shuttered by seven every evening.

vocab.n: Everyday and separable: knock it down. The formal equivalent is demolish; using both in one answer shows range without repetition.
vocab.eg: They knocked the old cinema down in a fortnight and put up something nobody can name.

vocab.def: the process by which a poor area becomes wealthier and its original residents are displaced
vocab.vi: quá trình thượng lưu hoá khu phố
vocab.n: Carefully neutral in form and critical in use. The displacement is the point; without it the word is being used loosely.
vocab.eg: Gentrification has made the area safer and pushed out most of the families who made it worth living in.

vocab.def: the useful facilities of a place: shops, transport, schools, parks
vocab.n: Almost always plural. Collocates with local, good and within walking distance of. Precise where facilities is vague.
vocab.eg: The flat itself is unremarkable; what sold it to me was the local amenities.

vocab.def: to settle somewhere with the intention of staying
vocab.vi: bén rễ, định cư lâu dài
vocab.n: Warm and slightly reflective. Ideal for the good place to live and continue living there questions.
vocab.eg: I've been here six years and I still haven't put down roots, which says something I'd rather not examine.

vocab.def: the noisy, energetic activity of a busy place
vocab.n: Fixed phrase, always with the, always in that order. Can be positive or negative depending on the verb — enjoy or escape.
vocab.eg: I go there precisely to escape the hustle and bustle for a few hours.

vocab.def: a city area dominated by buildings and lacking greenery
vocab.n: Vivid but very common among candidates, so it earns credit only when it is doing real work in a sentence rather than standing alone as a label.
vocab.eg: The district has turned into a concrete jungle, and the one surviving tree has its own fan page.

vocab.def: land in a town kept as parks, gardens or woodland
vocab.n: Planning vocabulary and precise. Collocates with public, preserve and a shortage of.
vocab.eg: The city has roughly two square metres of green space per resident, which you can feel in August.

vocab.def: full of large numbers of moving people or creatures
vocab.n: Implies movement, not just quantity. Teeming with tourists works; teeming with buildings does not.
vocab.eg: By seven in the evening the market is teeming with people and impossible to cross.

vocab.n: Negative but not harsh. Precise where old is ambiguous — an old building may be beautiful; a run-down one is not.
vocab.eg: The building is run-down in a way that's almost charming until you try to use the lift.

vocab.def: not changed or damaged by development or tourism
vocab.n: Carries an implied warning that it will not stay that way. British spelling; American English prefers unspoiled.
vocab.eg: It was still unspoilt when I went, which I suspect is no longer true.

vocab.def: pleasant and practical to live in
vocab.n: The standard term in urban policy and a strong Part 3 item. A liveable city is about daily practicality, not beauty.
vocab.eg: A liveable city isn't the one with the best skyline; it's the one where you don't need a car.

vocab.def: to have a view down over something
vocab.n: Beware the second meaning — to fail to notice. Context disambiguates, but a building overlooks, while a person overlooks a mistake.
vocab.eg: My grandmother's balcony overlooks the river, and she has spent forty years watching it change.

p1.q: Are there any things you don't like about your area?

b6.h: Name one thing and explain it
b6.f: One complaint → Why it matters → Concrete instance
pts: Choose one complaint, not three. A list of grievances is harder to develop than a single one explored properly.
Say what it costs you in practice — time, sleep, money — rather than simply calling it bad.
Keep the present simple for the ongoing situation; slip into the past only for a specific example.

b7.h: Balance the complaint so it sounds honest
b7.f: Complaint → Why it is worse than it sounds → Concession
pts: Explain why the problem is worse than an outsider would guess. That second layer is the development.
Add one less common item: an eyesore, run-down, the hustle and bustle, used once.
Concede something — though it's the price of living this centrally. An unqualified complaint sounds like a rant.

b8.h: Make the complaint reveal something about the city
b8.f: Reframe → Specific grievance → What it is a symptom of → Dry close
pts: Treat the annoyance as evidence of a wider pattern: planning, pace of growth, who the street is actually built for.
Admit your own complicity — you chose to live there, and for reasons that produced the problem.
Close short after the longer clauses. Understatement does more than emphasis here.

p2.q: Describe a quiet place that you would love to go to

b6.h: Cover the prompts and reach the time
b6.f: Where it is → How you know about it → What you would do → Why you want to go
pts: The card is hypothetical, so the spine is would. Drifting into the past simple answers a different card.
Two or three sentences per prompt, with the final one carrying most of the development.
Aim for at least ninety seconds. Under that, Fluency and Coherence is capped however accurate the language.

b7.h: Make the quiet concrete rather than abstract
b7.f: Why you need quiet → The place → What you would hear and do → What it would give you
pts: Open on why quiet has become something you have to go looking for. That frames everything after it.
Describe quiet through sound, not through its absence: the hum of something, a single distant noise.
Use second conditional and would perfect: I'd have taken a book I never finish.

b8.h: Let the place answer a question about your life
b8.f: In medias res → What you are escaping → The place, sensed → What you would not do there → Reflection
pts: Begin inside the wanting, not inside the description — the moment you last wished you were somewhere else.
Say what you would deliberately not do there. Absence is more revealing than activity.
Close on something the place would tell you about how you currently live, not on how nice it would be.

p3.q: Should cities preserve old buildings instead of replacing them?

b6.h: Take a side and support it
pts: Commit in the opening clause rather than saying both have advantages.
One reason about identity and one about practicality is enough structure here.
Name an actual building or street. A specific instance outperforms three general claims.

b7.f: It depends on which buildings → Case A → Case B → Governing principle
pts: Old buildings is not one category. Separate the genuinely historic from the merely old and decaying.
Raise cost honestly: preservation is expensive and somebody pays for it.
Close on a principle for deciding, not on it depends left hanging.

b8.h: Ask what preservation is actually preserving
b8.f: Reframe → Distinguish → Counter-example → Trade-off → Conditional verdict
pts: Separate preserving a building from preserving a way of living. Cities often keep the first and destroy the second.
Supply your own counter-example: a restored street that is now beautiful and has no residents left in it.
Name the trade-off in terms of who pays and who benefits, which is where this argument actually lives.
End on what would have to be true for you to support demolition.

critical.q: Should cities preserve old buildings instead of replacing them?

for.main: A city's buildings are the only continuous record most residents ever encounter, and once demolished the record cannot be reconstructed.
sup: Irreversibility. A new building can be built at any time; a two-hundred-year-old one cannot. Where a decision runs only one way, caution is simply rational.

Scale and texture. Old districts were built for people on foot, so they produce street life that modern blocks cannot replicate at any budget. What is lost is not the façade but the pavement in front of it.

Economic value arrives late. The quarters tourists pay to walk through were slums two generations ago. Cities that demolished theirs in the 1970s now build replicas, which is an expensive way to admit an error.

against.main: Preservation is usually argued by people who do not have to live in the buildings being preserved.
sup: Housing is the real shortage. A low-rise historic district occupies land that could house many times its current residents. Protecting it is a decision to price somebody out, and that decision is rarely stated.
Conditions. Picturesque frequently means damp, unsafe and impossible to heat or cool. Residents are asked to absorb a cost so that visitors can enjoy a view.

Cities are not museums. Every admired historic quarter was once a demolition that offended its own generation. Freezing a city at one arbitrary moment denies the next generation what the last one had.

critical.verdict: The Band 8 resolution: the question is badly posed, because preserving a building and preserving a neighbourhood are different projects and often opposed. A restored street with no original residents has preserved the architecture and demolished the thing that made it worth keeping. The defensible position is to protect fabric where it still carries a living community, and to accept replacement where it does not — while being honest that the alternative is almost always who can afford to stay.

models.q: Describe a quiet place that you would love to go to
models.html:
I would like to talk about a quiet place that I want to visit. It is a small island in the north of Vietnam called Quan Lan.

I know about this place because my friend went there last year and showed me many photos. She said it is very peaceful and there are not many tourists. The beaches are clean and the water is very blue.

If I go there, I would walk on the beach, read books and take photos. I would also like to try the seafood because it is fresh. I think I would go with my sister because she also likes quiet places.

I want to go there because my life in the city is very busy and noisy. I need to relax and have time for myself. So I hope I can visit it next summer.
models.len: about 72 seconds — below the required range

notes.fc: The four prompts are answered in order and the organisation is perfectly clear, but the scaffolding is audible and the opening formula announces preparation. It ends at seventy-two seconds, and an answer that stops before ninety has not demonstrated speaking at length, which caps this criterion regardless of accuracy.
notes.lr: Peaceful, clean, very blue, busy and noisy, relax. Accurate and sufficient, with nothing less common anywhere. Very appears three times.
notes.gr: One mixed conditional error: If I go there, I would walk switches from first to second conditional mid-sentence. Otherwise simple and compound sentences, controlled, with no relative clause and no perfect aspect.
notes.pr: Clear and easy to follow. Stress falls on content words but the delivery is even throughout, so the shift from describing the island to explaining why it matters is not audible.

models.prosody: I would LIKE to talk‿about‿a QUIet place / that‿I want to VIsit ↘
models.tip: Two fixes together would lift this to about 6.5. Make the conditional consistent — If I went there, I'd walk… — and replace the opening sentence with the reason you want to go. The same content then starts at the interesting end.

models.q: Describe a quiet place that you would love to go to
models.html:
I've started noticing how rarely I'm anywhere genuinely quiet, which is probably why this particular place has been sitting in the back of my mind for about a year.

It's a small island called Quan Lan, up in the north-east, and a friend of mine went there two winters ago and came back slightly evangelical about it. What she described wasn't the beach — it was the fact that at six in the morning she could hear her own footsteps on the sand. That stayed with me.

If I did go, I think I'd deliberately not plan anything. I'd take a book I've been failing to finish since March, and I'd probably spend the first day simply not checking my phone, which would be harder than it sounds. I'd go with my sister, who is the only person I know who doesn't fill silences.

The real reason is that I live somewhere teeming with people and I've stopped noticing it, and I suspect I'd only understand how loud my ordinary week is once I'd spent three days somewhere it wasn't.

notes.fc: The turn opens on the need rather than on the place, and the four prompts are all answered without any of them being visible as a prompt. The markers vary in function — explaining, contrasting, concluding — and the long turn is produced without noticeable effort.
notes.lr: Slightly evangelical, stayed with me, failing to finish, teeming with people, fill silences. Less common items appear naturally and the dry humour of slightly evangelical shows register awareness.
notes.gr: Second conditional held consistently (if I did go, I'd…), a non-defining relative clause, and a past perfect inside a conditional in the final sentence. Error-free with genuine variety.
notes.pr: The pause before she could hear her own footsteps on the sand creates the image rather than merely stating it. That stayed with me is short and falls, marking it as the point of the paragraph.

models.prosody: I've started NOticing / how RAREly‿I'm‿anywhere genuinely QUIet ↘ ‖ (pause) which‿is probably WHY this particular place / has been sitting‿in the BACK of my mind ↗ / for‿about‿a YEAR ↘
models.tip: Three links to rehearse: anywhere‿I'm, spent three days somewhere‿it wasn't, and checking my phone, which‿would be. Each joins a final consonant to a following vowel; without them the sentences sound assembled rather than spoken.

models.q: Describe a quiet place that you would love to go to
models.html:
Last Tuesday I stood on my balcony at eleven at night and counted four separate sources of noise. That's the context for this answer.

The place is a small island called Quan Lan, a few hours north-east of here, still more or less unspoilt — though I'm aware that saying so is part of the process by which places stop being unspoilt. A friend went two winters ago and came back describing not the beach but the silence, which I found I envied more than I expected to.

What I'd want there isn't really an activity, which is the awkward part of the question. I'd take a book I've been failing to finish since March and probably not finish it there either. What I'd actually be doing is finding out whether I can sit still — something I used to be able to do and apparently can't any more. I'd go with my sister, who is the only person I know capable of not filling a silence.

And I suspect the point isn't the island at all. Had somebody offered me three quiet days ten years ago I'd have found them tedious; the fact that I now find the idea almost luxurious tells me rather more about the last decade than about Quan Lan. Which is, I think, why I keep not booking it.
models.len: about 120 seconds — stopped by the examiner

notes.fc: Two short sentences establish the whole frame before the place is mentioned. All four prompts are addressed and none is audible as a prompt. The closing clause reverses the answer's own premise, and the pauses throughout are clearly spent selecting ideas rather than retrieving language.
notes.lr: More or less unspoilt, part of the process by which, envied more than I expected to, almost luxurious, capable of not filling a silence. The parenthetical about saying a place is unspoilt being what ruins it is doing conceptual work, not decoration.
notes.gr: Conditional inversion (Had somebody offered me), a cleft (What I'd actually be doing is…), a semicolon joining two independent clauses in contrast, and a sentence-initial Which used deliberately as a fragment. Structures change with rhetorical function; errors are absent.
notes.pr: The opening demands flat, factual delivery on counted four separate sources of noise so that That's the context for this answer can land dry. The final fragment slows and falls, and the self-deprecation in why I keep not booking it is carried entirely by intonation rather than by any word in it.

models.prosody: Last TUESday / I stood‿on my BALcony‿at‿eleven‿at NIGHT / and counted FOUR separate sources‿of NOISE ↘ ‖ (pause 0.5s) That's the CONtext for this‿answer ↘↘
models.tip: Everything depends on the opening pair. The first sentence must be delivered absolutely flat, like a fact being reported, and the second must drop lower and slower. If the first sentence is given any emotional colour, the second has nothing to contrast with and the joke disappears. Record only those two sentences until the difference is obvious on playback.
